title: Rejected at Home, a Prophet Beheaded, Bread in the Wilderness
summary: Jesus is rejected in his hometown of Nazareth, then sends the Twelve out two by two to preach repentance and heal. Mark pauses to tell how Herod Antipas had John the Baptist beheaded at a banquet. When the apostles return, Jesus feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, walks on the sea to his struggling disciples, and heals crowds at Gennesaret.
story: Chapters 4 and 5 showed Jesus' authority over the sea, demons, disease, and death, and ended with a dead girl raised to life. Chapter 6 turns to how people respond to that authority. His own town takes offense, a king mistakes him for John come back from the dead, and even his disciples, who have just been sharing his work, fail to understand what they have seen. The chapter opens the section of Mark scholars often call the bread section (6:7 to 8:26), where loaves, meals, and blindness recur until Peter's confession in chapter 8. It also casts a shadow forward: John's death at the hands of a ruler who respected him but would not defy his guests is a preview of what will happen to Jesus under Pilate.
historical:
The Herod of this chapter is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. Rome gave him the title tetrarch, a ruler of part of a kingdom, not king; Mark's “King Herod” may reflect popular usage, or a touch of irony, since Antipas later sought the royal title and was exiled for it instead. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, also tells of John's execution. He says Antipas imprisoned John at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and killed him because he feared John's influence over the crowds might lead to revolt. Mark's account gives the personal motive, Josephus the political one, and the two are compatible: a prophet who condemned the ruler's marriage was also a public threat.

The marriage itself was a scandal. Antipas divorced his first wife, a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV, to marry Herodias, who had been the wife of his half-brother. Josephus reports that Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle and that some Jews saw the defeat as God's judgment for John's death. Josephus names Herodias's first husband simply as Herod, while Mark calls him Philip; some scholars see an error, others suggest the man bore both names, as members of the Herodian family often did. Josephus also gives the name of Herodias's daughter, Salome, which Mark does not.
cultural:
Nazareth was a small village, and its people knew Jesus' family and trade. The word translated carpenter (tekton) covers a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Calling a man the son of his mother rather than his father was unusual and may hint at the rumors surrounding his birth, or simply that Joseph had died. The brothers and sisters named here have been understood in three ways: as later children of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view), as children of Joseph from an earlier marriage (the view of much of the Eastern church), or as cousins (a view associated with Jerome and common in the Western Catholic tradition).

The instructions to the Twelve assume Jewish hospitality: travelers depended on households that would take them in. Shaking dust off the feet was a gesture some Jews used when leaving Gentile territory; applied to a Jewish town, it treats that place as having shut itself out. Anointing the sick with oil was a common remedy and here a sign of healing (compare James 5:14). Herod's oath before his nobles bound him in an honor culture where public words could not be taken back without shame. A denarius was roughly a day's wage for a laborer, so two hundred denarii was most of a year's income. The fourth watch of the night, by Roman reckoning, ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.
literary: Mark uses one of his sandwiches here: the Twelve are sent out (verses 7 to 13), the story of John's death fills the gap (14 to 29), and they return (30). The frame links mission and martyrdom, since those who preach repentance may meet John's end. The feeding is told with Old Testament echoes: the wilderness place recalls Israel fed with manna, the sheep without a shepherd recall Moses' prayer in Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34, and the groups of hundreds and fifties recall Israel's ordering in Exodus 18:21. The words took, blessed, broke, and gave anticipate the Last Supper in chapter 14. The sea crossing has its own echoes: Jesus intends to pass by them, as God passed by Moses and Elijah on the mountain (Exodus 33:19-22, 1 Kings 19:11), and his words “Take courage! It is I” use the Greek phrase ego eimi, which also stands behind God's name in Exodus 3:14.

outline.t: The Twelve sent out two by two
The death of John the Baptist
The apostles return and five thousand are fed

doctrines.note: Unbelief in Nazareth limits what Jesus does there, and the disciples' hardened hearts keep them from understanding the loaves. Faith in Mark is not a technique that produces miracles but a trust that receives what Jesus offers; its absence closes the door from the human side.

Jesus shares his authority with the Twelve and sends them to preach repentance, travel light, and depend on others' hospitality. Mark calls them apostles, those sent, only here, when they return from their first mission.
John's death shows the cost of speaking God's word to power. Mark places it at the center of the disciples' first mission, so that the reader learns early that faithful witness can end in a prison.
The feeding and the sea crossing present Jesus as the shepherd Israel lacked and as the one who does what God alone does, providing bread in the wilderness and walking on the waters.

words.note: Splagchnizomai, to have compassion. The word comes from the noun for the inner organs, where ancient people located deep feeling, and describes pity felt in the gut. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus or of figures in his parables who stand for God. Here it moves him to teach and feed a crowd that interrupted his rest.

Skandalizo, to cause to stumble or to take offense. The noun skandalon is a snare or stumbling block. The people of Nazareth trip over Jesus' ordinariness: they know his trade and his family. Mark uses the same verb in 14:27 when Jesus predicts that all the disciples will fall away.

Poroo, to harden, from a word for a callus or a stone. Mark applies it not to Jesus' opponents (compare 3:5) but to his own disciples (verse 52, and again in 8:17). Hardness of heart in Scripture is a settled incapacity to perceive, and Mark is honest that insiders suffer from it too.

Tekton, a craftsman or builder, most often in wood but also in stone. Only here is Jesus himself called a tekton; Matthew 13:55 calls him the carpenter's son. It placed him among ordinary working men, which is exactly why his hometown could not accept his wisdom.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as prophet, shepherd, and more than either. He accepts the prophet's lot of rejection at home, and John's fate foreshadows his own. He has compassion on a leaderless people and feeds them in the wilderness, as God fed Israel with manna, and the language of taking, blessing, breaking, and giving points ahead to the bread he will give as his body. On the sea he does what the Old Testament reserves for God, who alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8), and he names himself with words that echo the divine name. The disciples do not yet understand, which is part of Mark's point: who Jesus is cannot be fully grasped until the cross and resurrection explain the bread.

hard.q: Mark says Jesus could not perform miracles in Nazareth. Was his power limited by people's unbelief?
hard.a: Mark's wording is blunt, and Matthew's parallel softens it to say he did not do many miracles there because of their unbelief (Matthew 13:58). Interpreters have read the statement in several ways. One view is that Jesus' miracles were never displays forced on unwilling people but acts that met faith, so where no one came to him in trust there was little for him to do; the few sick he did heal were presumably those who came. Another stresses that could not here describes moral rather than physical impossibility: it would not fit his mission to perform wonders for a crowd that had already decided against him, much as he later refuses to give a sign on demand (8:12). A third notes that in his incarnate life Jesus chose to work in dependence on the Father and the Spirit, and that Mark does not hesitate to show his real humanity, including his amazement at their unbelief in verse 6. None of these readings means that human unbelief overpowers God. They mean that Jesus' power is personal and relational, exercised for those who receive him, and that refusing him has real consequences.

questions: The people of Nazareth could not accept wisdom from someone they thought they already knew. Where might familiarity keep you from hearing God speak?
Herod listened gladly to John and still killed him to save face before his guests. What pressures make it hard for you to act on what you know is right?
The disciples had just seen the loaves and still did not understand. What past experiences of God's provision are you in danger of forgetting when the wind is against you?
